decks.title: Biomolecules — Part 1: Carbohydrates, amino acids and proteins
goals: Classify carbohydrates into mono-, di- and polysaccharides and state one function of each given sugar
Draw glycine, alanine and serine, explain the zwitterion and classify amino acids
Describe the four levels of protein structure, the bonds that stabilise each and the functions of proteins

slides.heading: Carbohydrates, amino acids and proteins
slides.body_md: Part 1: the sugars that fuel and build cells, and the amino acids that are joined into proteins.

visual.alt: Path from carbohydrates to amino acids to proteins

slides.narration: Cells are made of a few kinds of large molecules. We begin with carbohydrates, which supply energy and build structures, and then study amino acids and the proteins that are built from them.

slides.heading: Classes of carbohydrates
slides.body_md: Carbohydrates are classified by the number of sugar units joined together.

rows: Glucose is the main fuel; ribose and deoxyribose form part of RNA and DNA
Dietary sugars; broken down to monosaccharides
Stores of energy and structural materials

visual.alt: Table of the three classes of carbohydrates

slides.narration: One sugar unit makes a monosaccharide, two make a disaccharide, and many make a polysaccharide. Glucose is the common fuel, while ribose and deoxyribose are the sugars of the nucleic acids.

slides.heading: How disaccharides are formed
slides.body_md: Two monosaccharides join by a **glycosidic bond**, and one molecule of **water** is lost.

slides.narration: Maltose is two glucose units joined together. Lactose, the sugar of milk, is glucose joined to galactose. Sucrose, cane sugar, is glucose joined to fructose. Each joining releases one molecule of water.

slides.heading: Polysaccharides
slides.body_md: Polysaccharides are long chains of sugar units; their linkages decide their function.

rows: Reserve food of animals, in liver and muscle
Structural material of plant cell walls
Reserve food in roots and tubers such as dahlia
Wall of fungi and the outer skeleton of arthropods

visual.alt: Table of polysaccharides

slides.narration: Starch and glycogen are stores of glucose, in plants and animals. Cellulose also contains glucose, but joined differently, so it forms strong walls that humans cannot digest. Inulin stores fructose, and chitin builds fungal walls and insect skeletons.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: hydrolysing sucrose
slides.body_md: The mass of one mole of sucrose is 342 grams and that of glucose or fructose 180 grams. How much water is needed to hydrolyse 171 grams of sucrose, and how much glucose and fructose are formed?
bullets: Moles of sucrose = 171 ÷ 342 = 0.5.
One mole of sucrose takes up one mole of water (18 grams), so water used = 0.5 × 18 = 9 grams.
Glucose formed = 0.5 × 180 = 90 grams, and fructose also 90 grams, a total of 180 grams.

visual.alt: Worked table: 9 grams of water used, 180 grams of sugars formed

slides.narration: Hydrolysis adds water. Half a mole of sucrose takes up half a mole of water and gives half a mole each of glucose and fructose. The mass of the sugars formed equals the mass of sucrose plus the water used.

slides.heading: Classes of amino acids
slides.body_md: Amino acids are grouped by their R groups and by whether the body can make them.

rows: One amino and one carboxyl group
Extra carboxyl group in the R group
Extra amino or basic group in the R group
Not made by the body; must come from food
Valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan

visual.alt: Table of the classes of amino acids

slides.narration: Acidic amino acids have a second carboxyl group, basic ones an extra amino group, and two contain sulphur. Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body, so they must be supplied by food.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: building a peptide
slides.body_md: Glycine weighs 75, alanine 89 and serine 105 (in daltons), and water 18. Find the mass of the tripeptide made of these three, joined once each, and how many different tripeptides can be made from them.
bullets: Sum of residues = 75 + 89 + 105 = 269.
Two peptide bonds form, releasing two waters: 269 − 2 × 18 = 233.
Three different residues can be ordered in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways, so 6 different tripeptides exist. With all twenty amino acids the number would be 20 × 20 × 20 = 8000.

visual.alt: Worked table: mass 233, 6 orders

slides.narration: Each peptide bond removes one water. Three residues need two bonds, so the tripeptide weighs two waters less than the three amino acids separately. Changing the order gives a different peptide, so there are six.

slides.narration: The primary structure is the order of amino acids. The chain then coils into a helix or folds into a sheet, which is the secondary structure. The whole chain folds into the tertiary structure, and several folded chains may join in the quaternary structure.

slides.heading: Bonds and functions of proteins
slides.body_md: Each level is held by its own kind of bond; the final shape decides the function.

rows: Hydrogen bonds, ionic and hydrophobic interactions, disulphide bridges between cysteines
Enzymes, structure (collagen, keratin), transport (haemoglobin), hormones (insulin), defence (antibodies), movement (actin, myosin)

visual.alt: Table of the bonds and functions of proteins

slides.narration: Peptide bonds hold the primary structure. Hydrogen bonds hold the helix and the sheet. The tertiary shape is held by several kinds of bond, including disulphide bridges between cysteines. Proteins act as enzymes and as structural, transport, hormone and defence molecules.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: counting bonds in a protein
slides.body_md: A protein is made of four separate polypeptide chains and has two hundred and eighty amino acids in all. How many peptide bonds does it contain, and how many water molecules were released in making it?
bullets: A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds, so four chains of total length 280 have 280 − 4 = 276 bonds.
Each bond releases one water, so 276 waters were released.
The four chains are held together by weak bonds, not peptide bonds: this is the quaternary structure.

visual.alt: Worked table: 276 peptide bonds

slides.narration: For each separate chain, the number of peptide bonds is one less than the number of amino acids. So subtract the number of chains from the total. The bonds between chains are weaker links and are not counted.

slides.heading: Quick check: protein structure
slides.body_md: Which bonds mainly hold the secondary structure of a protein?
slides.narration: Quick check. What kind of bond holds a helix in shape?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, ribose, deoxyribose), disaccharides (maltose, lactose, sucrose), polysaccharides (glycogen, starch, cellulose, inulin, chitin).
Disaccharides form by a glycosidic bond with loss of water.
Amino acid: amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and R group; zwitterion in water; acidic, basic, neutral, sulphur-containing; essential and non-essential.
Proteins: primary (peptide bonds), secondary (hydrogen bonds), tertiary (several bonds), quaternary (subunits).

rows: n amino acids in one chain

visual.alt: Summary table of key points

slides.narration: To recap: sugars join by glycosidic bonds with loss of water; an amino acid exists as a zwitterion in water; and a protein is built in four levels, each with its own kind of bond.

slides.heading: Lipids, enzymes and secondary metabolites
slides.body_md: Part 2: fats and oils, the enzymes that run the chemistry of life, and the extra chemicals made by plants.

visual.alt: Path from lipids to enzymes to secondary metabolites

slides.narration: Fats store energy and build membranes. Enzymes speed up nearly every reaction in the cell. And plants make many extra chemicals, the secondary metabolites, that serve them in other ways.

slides.heading: Classes and functions of lipids
slides.body_md: Lipids are insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents.

rows: Fatty acids, glycerol, steroids such as cholesterol

visual.alt: Table of the classes of lipids

slides.narration: Simple lipids such as fats, oils and waxes store energy and insulate. Phospholipids form membranes, and steroids such as cholesterol act as hormones or help in membranes. All are insoluble in water.

slides.heading: Fats and oils
slides.body_md: A **triglyceride** is one glycerol joined to three fatty acids by **ester bonds**. **Fats** are solid and **saturated**; **oils** are liquid and **unsaturated**.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: mass and energy of a fat
slides.body_md: Glycerol weighs 92, palmitic acid 256 and oleic acid 282. Find the mass of tripalmitin and of triolein, and compare the energy in twenty grams of fat and of carbohydrate (nine and four kilocalories per gram).
bullets: Triolein = 92 + 3 × 282 − 3 × 18 = 884. Oleic acid has 1 double bond, so it has 2 hydrogen atoms fewer than stearic acid.
Energy: 20 g of fat gives 180 kilocalories; 20 g of carbohydrate gives 80, so fat gives 2.25 times as much.

visual.alt: Worked table: tripalmitin, triolein and energy values

slides.narration: Three water molecules are lost when glycerol joins three fatty acids. Fat gives more than twice the energy of the same mass of carbohydrate, which is why animals store energy as fat.

slides.heading: Enzymes: properties and naming
slides.body_md: Enzymes are biological catalysts, almost all of them proteins.

rows: Lower the activation energy; not used up
Each acts on one substrate or a closely related group, through its active site
Work best at an optimum temperature and pH; denatured by extremes
Can speed up a reaction in either direction
Name of substrate or reaction plus -ase: lactase, lipase, dehydrogenase

visual.alt: Table of the properties and naming of enzymes

slides.narration: An enzyme lowers the energy needed to start a reaction and is not used up. It is specific because of the shape of its active site. Most enzyme names end in a-s-e, built from the substrate or the type of reaction.

slides.heading: Six classes of enzymes
slides.body_md: Enzymes are classified by the type of reaction they catalyse.

rows: Transfer of electrons or hydrogen: oxidation and reduction
Transfer of a group, such as phosphate
Removing a group without water, leaving a double bond
Rearranging a molecule into its isomer

visual.alt: Table of the six classes of enzymes

slides.narration: Oxidoreductases move electrons, transferases move groups, hydrolases use water to split bonds, lyases split without water, isomerases rearrange, and ligases join molecules using energy from ATP.

slides.heading: Cofactors
slides.body_md: Many enzymes need a non-protein part. The protein alone is the **apoenzyme**; with its cofactor it is the **holoenzyme**.

rows: Organic, tightly bound to the enzyme
Organic, loosely bound; often made from a vitamin

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of cofactor

slides.narration: A prosthetic group stays attached to the enzyme. A coenzyme is a loosely attached organic helper, often built from a vitamin. Metal ions such as zinc and magnesium also activate many enzymes.

slides.heading: Effect of temperature, pH and substrate
slides.body_md: Each enzyme has an **optimum temperature** and **optimum pH**; rate rises with substrate until it reaches a maximum.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading enzyme rates
slides.body_md: For an enzyme, the maximum rate is 80 units and the Michaelis constant is 10. Find the rate at substrate concentrations of 10, 20 and 30, and say what the constant means.
bullets: Rate = maximum × S ÷ (constant + S). At 10: 80 × 10 ÷ 20 = 40.
At 20: 80 × 20 ÷ 30 = 53.3, which is half of the maximum, because the concentration equals the constant.
The constant is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of the maximum.

slides.narration: At the point where the rate is half the maximum, the substrate concentration equals the constant. Above it the curve flattens, since nearly all enzyme molecules are already busy.

slides.body_md: A **competitive inhibitor** resembles the substrate and **blocks the active site**; more substrate **overcomes** it. Example: **malonate** and **succinic dehydrogenase**.

slides.heading: Secondary metabolites
slides.body_md: **Secondary metabolites** are compounds that are not directly needed for growth, development or reproduction, but help the plant in other ways.

slides.narration: Secondary metabolites are not part of the basic chemistry of the cell. Alkaloids defend plants and are used as drugs. Pigments attract animals, and gums seal wounds. Many are valuable to humans.

bullets: Lipids: fats (saturated, solid) and oils (unsaturated, liquid); triglyceride = glycerol + three fatty acids; functions: energy, insulation, membranes, hormones.

sections.heading: 1. Carbohydrates
sections.body_md:
**Carbohydrates** are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones (or compounds that give them on hydrolysis) and are classified by the number of sugar units.

**Monosaccharides** cannot be hydrolysed further: **glucose** (the main fuel, mass 180), **ribose** and **deoxyribose** (sugars of RNA and DNA; deoxyribose has one oxygen fewer, 150 against 134), also fructose and galactose.

**Disaccharides** are two monosaccharides joined by a **glycosidic bond** with loss of a water molecule: **maltose** = glucose + glucose; **lactose** = glucose + galactose (milk sugar); **sucrose** = glucose + fructose (cane sugar). Each has a mass of 342. Maltose and lactose are **reducing sugars** (they reduce Benedict’s solution); sucrose is **non-reducing** until it is hydrolysed. Hydrolysis of 171 g of sucrose takes up 9 g of water and gives 90 g of glucose and 90 g of fructose.

**Polysaccharides** are long chains of monosaccharides:
- **Starch** — reserve food of plants (glucose units).
- **Glycogen** — reserve food of animals, in liver and muscle; highly branched glucose polymer.
- **Cellulose** — structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls; glucose units joined differently from starch, so humans cannot digest it.
- **Inulin** — polymer of fructose; a reserve in tubers and roots such as dahlia and chicory.
- **Chitin** — polymer of an amino sugar; wall of fungi and exoskeleton of arthropods.

Sugar with a free aldehyde or ketone group that reduces Benedict’s solution.

sections.heading: 2. Amino acids
sections.body_md:
**Amino acids** are the monomers of proteins. Each has an **amino group**, a **carboxyl group**, a **hydrogen** atom and an **R group** attached to the same (alpha) carbon. They differ only in R: **glycine** (R = H, 75), **alanine** (R = CH₃, 89) and **serine** (R = CH₂OH, 105).

In water, the carboxyl group gives up a proton to the amino group, so the molecule carries both a positive (NH₃⁺) and a negative (COO⁻) charge and no net charge: a **zwitterion**. In acid it carries a net positive charge, and in alkali a net negative charge.

**Classes by R group:** **neutral** (glycine, alanine, serine, valine); **acidic** (aspartic acid and glutamic acid, with an extra carboxyl group); **basic** (lysine, arginine, histidine); **sulphur-containing** (cysteine, methionine). **Essential** amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from food: valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine and tryptophan (histidine is also essential for infants). **Non-essential** ones such as glycine, alanine and serine can be made.

A peptide bond joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the next, releasing water. The tripeptide of glycine, alanine and serine weighs 233 (269 − 2 × 18).

sections.heading: 3. Proteins
sections.body_md:
**Proteins** are polymers of amino acids. Four levels of structure:
- **Primary** — the sequence of amino acids joined by **peptide bonds** (covalent). A change of one amino acid can change the function of the protein.
- **Secondary** — regular folding of the chain into an **α-helix** or **β-pleated sheet**, held by **hydrogen bonds** between backbone groups.
- **Tertiary** — folding of the whole chain into a three-dimensional shape, held by hydrogen bonds, **ionic** and **hydrophobic** interactions and **disulphide bridges** between cysteines.
- **Quaternary** — association of two or more folded polypeptide chains (subunits) by weak bonds, as in haemoglobin.

**Denaturation** (by heat, acid or alkali) breaks the weak bonds and unfolds the protein, but the peptide bonds of the primary structure stay intact. **Functions:** enzymes, structure (collagen, keratin), transport (haemoglobin), hormones (insulin), defence (antibodies), contraction (actin, myosin), storage (casein).

A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds; a protein of 280 amino acids in 4 chains has 276.

sections.heading: 4. Lipids
sections.body_md:
**Lipids** are insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents. **Simple lipids:** **fats**, **oils** (esters of glycerol and fatty acids) and **waxes**. **Compound lipids:** **phospholipids** and glycolipids. **Derived lipids:** fatty acids, glycerol and **steroids** such as cholesterol.

A **triglyceride** is glycerol (mass 92) joined to three fatty acids by **ester bonds** with loss of three water molecules; tripalmitin weighs 806. **Saturated** fatty acids have no double bonds, so the chains pack closely and the **fat is solid** at room temperature (usually animal fats); **unsaturated** fatty acids have one or more double bonds that bend the chain, so the **oil is liquid** (usually plant oils).

**Functions:** energy store (about 9 kcal per gram, more than twice that of carbohydrate), insulation, protection of organs, waterproofing (wax), structure of membranes (phospholipids, cholesterol) and hormones (steroids).

sections.heading: 5. Enzymes
sections.body_md:
**Enzymes** are biological catalysts, almost all proteins. They **lower the activation energy**, are **specific** (active site), are **not used up**, act in small amounts under mild conditions and can act in both directions. Names usually end in **-ase** (substrate or reaction type).

**Six classes:** **oxidoreductases** (oxidation and reduction; lactate dehydrogenase), **transferases** (transfer of a group; hexokinase), **hydrolases** (hydrolysis; lipase, lactase), **lyases** (removal of a group without water; decarboxylase), **isomerases** (rearrangement; glucose phosphate isomerase), **ligases** (joining using ATP; DNA ligase).

**Cofactors.** The protein part is the **apoenzyme**; with its cofactor it is the **holoenzyme**. **Prosthetic group:** organic, tightly bound (haem in catalase). **Coenzyme:** organic, loosely bound, often from a vitamin (NAD from niacin). **Metal ions:** zinc, magnesium.

**Effects.** Activity rises with **temperature** to an optimum (about 37 °C for a human enzyme; 8, 16, 30, 49, 70, 88, 100, 17, 0 per cent at 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 37, 45 and 55 °C in the model) and then falls as the enzyme is denatured; each enzyme has an **optimum pH** (pepsin about 2, trypsin about 8). With rising **substrate** the rate increases to a maximum (80 units in the model; 26.7, 40, 53.3, 66.7, 72.7, 76.2 at substrate 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200).

**Competitive inhibition.** An inhibitor resembling the substrate occupies the active site; the maximum rate is unchanged but a higher substrate concentration is needed (16, 26.7, 40, 57.1, 66.7, 72.7 with the inhibitor). Example: **malonate** inhibits **succinic dehydrogenase** because it resembles succinate.

Substance resembling the substrate that blocks the active site.

sections.heading: 6. Secondary metabolites
sections.body_md:
**Primary metabolites** (sugars, amino acids, lipids, nucleotides) take part in the basic life of the cell. **Secondary metabolites** are compounds that are **not directly needed for growth, development or reproduction**, but have ecological and economic importance.

**Examples:** **alkaloids** (morphine, quinine, nicotine, caffeine) — defence against herbivores and medicines; **pigments** (carotenoids, anthocyanins) — colour to attract pollinators and animals that spread seeds; **gums** (gum arabic) and resins — seal wounds; **terpenoids** such as essential oils, rubber; toxins (abrin, ricin) and drugs (vinblastin, curcumin).

key_terms.definition_md: Compound not directly needed for growth or reproduction but useful to the organism in other ways.
Nitrogen-containing secondary metabolite such as morphine.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying sucrose is glucose plus glucose (it is glucose plus fructose; maltose is glucose plus glucose).
- Writing that a zwitterion has no charges (it has two, with no net charge).
- Giving hydrogen bonds for the primary structure (peptide bonds); or peptide bonds for the secondary structure.
- Saying that boiling breaks the peptide bonds of a protein (it unfolds the shape).
- Saying a competitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate (it raises the substrate needed for half the maximum; the maximum is the same).
- Confusing a coenzyme (loosely bound) with a prosthetic group (tightly bound).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a monomer, a bond, a class of enzyme, a cofactor, give-a-reason and analogy.
- 2–3-mark questions: structures of glycine, alanine and serine; zwitterion; saturated and unsaturated fats; classes of enzymes; graphs of activity.
- 5-mark questions in parts: protein structure with bonds; enzyme properties with graphs; competitive inhibition with malonate.

questions.stem_md: Which polysaccharide is a reserve of fructose units in a dahlia tuber?
questions.solution_md: Inulin is a polymer of fructose and a reserve in tubers such as dahlia — option (a).

questions.stem_md: What is the net charge on an amino acid that exists as a zwitterion?

options.text_md: Positive, because the amino group is charged
Zero, because one positive and one negative charge are present
Negative, because the carboxyl group is charged
It depends only on the R group

questions.solution_md: The two charges cancel, so the net charge is zero — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which bonds mainly hold the secondary structure of a protein?

options.text_md: Hydrogen bonds between groups of the polypeptide backbone

questions.solution_md: An α-helix or a β-sheet is held by hydrogen bonds — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Why is a plant oil liquid at room temperature?

options.text_md: Its fatty acids have no double bonds
Its fatty acids have double bonds that bend the chains so that they cannot pack closely
It is made of amino acids

questions.solution_md: Double bonds kink the chains of an unsaturated oil — option (c).

questions.stem_md: To which class does an enzyme that breaks a bond by adding water belong?
questions.solution_md: Hydrolases split bonds by hydrolysis — option (a).

questions.stem_md: What happens to the rate of an enzyme reaction containing a competitive inhibitor when the substrate concentration is made very high?

options.text_md: It approaches the maximum rate of the uninhibited reaction
It stays far below the uninhibited maximum

questions.solution_md: Substrate outcompetes the inhibitor, so the maximum rate is almost reached — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A sugar solution gives no brick-red colour with Benedict’s solution, but it does after being boiled with a few drops of dilute acid. The sugar is most likely
questions.solution_md: Sucrose is non-reducing until acid hydrolyses it to glucose and fructose; the other sugars reduce Benedict’s solution directly — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A child lacks the enzyme lactase and cannot digest the sugar of milk. When that sugar is hydrolysed by lactase, which products are formed?
questions.solution_md: Lactose is glucose joined to galactose — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Humans digest starch but not cellulose, although both are made only of glucose. The difference lies in

options.text_md: the way in which the glucose units are linked
the number of carbon atoms in each unit
the presence of nitrogen in cellulose
the solubility of glucose in water

questions.solution_md: The different linkage between glucose units makes cellulose indigestible to human enzymes — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Deoxyribose, the sugar of DNA, differs from ribose, the sugar of RNA, in having

options.text_md: a nitrogen atom in its ring
one oxygen atom fewer, since carbon 2 has no hydroxyl group
a phosphate group attached to it

questions.solution_md: Ribose is C5H10O5 (150) and deoxyribose C5H10O4 (134): one oxygen fewer — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sucrose does not reduce Benedict’s solution until it has been boiled with dilute acid.

**Reason (R):** Boiling with acid hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose, which are reducing sugars.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the hydrolysis to reducing sugars explains the change — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Plants store glucose as starch and not as free glucose.

answer.model_answer_md: Starch is **insoluble** and **osmotically inactive**, so large amounts can be stored without drawing water into the cell, whereas free glucose is soluble.

questions.solution_md: Insoluble, osmotically inactive.

questions.stem_md: The molar mass of sucrose is 342 g and that of water is 18 g. How many grams of water are used to hydrolyse 684 g of sucrose?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{684}{342} = 2$ mol of sucrose; each mole takes up one mole of water, so $2 \times 18 = 36$ g.

questions.stem_md: State the monosaccharides that make up maltose and sucrose, and name the bond that joins the two units in a disaccharide.

answer.model_answer_md: **Maltose** is made of **two glucose** units, and **sucrose** of **glucose and fructose**. In a disaccharide the two units are joined by a **glycosidic bond**, formed with the loss of one molecule of water.

questions.solution_md: Maltose; sucrose; glycosidic bond.

marking_scheme.step: Glycosidic bond with loss of water

questions.stem_md: A student has samples of glucose, lactose and glycogen. Classify each as a mono-, di- or polysaccharide and state one function of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Glucose** is a **monosaccharide**; it is the main **fuel** of cells. **Lactose** is a **disaccharide** (glucose and galactose) and is the **sugar of milk**, a food for the young. **Glycogen** is a **polysaccharide** of glucose and is the **reserve food of animals**, stored in liver and muscle.

questions.solution_md: Class and function of each.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish starch from cellulose in terms of where each is found, its role and whether humans can digest it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Starch** is found in **plant storage organs** such as seeds and tubers and is a **reserve food**; humans **digest** it with amylase. **Cellulose** is found in **plant cell walls** and is a **structural** material; humans **cannot digest** it because their enzymes cannot split the linkage between its glucose units, although it adds fibre to the diet.

questions.solution_md: Site, role, digestibility.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the three classes of carbohydrates according to the number of sugar units, giving two examples of each. [2]
(b) Give the source or the function of inulin, cellulose, glycogen and chitin. [2]
(c) Why is sucrose called a non-reducing sugar? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Monosaccharides** (glucose, ribose), **disaccharides** (maltose, lactose, sucrose) and **polysaccharides** (starch, glycogen, cellulose, inulin, chitin).

(b) **Inulin**: a fructose reserve in roots and tubers such as dahlia. **Cellulose**: structural material of plant cell walls. **Glycogen**: reserve food of animals in liver and muscle. **Chitin**: wall of fungi and exoskeleton of arthropods.

(c) In **sucrose** the reducing groups of both glucose and fructose are **tied up in the glycosidic bond**, so it does not reduce Benedict’s solution unless hydrolysed.

questions.solution_md: Classes; polysaccharides; non-reducing.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Four polysaccharides, half a mark each

questions.stem_md: A solution of glycine is made strongly alkaline. Compared with the zwitterion, the glycine molecules now carry

options.text_md: a net positive charge, because the carboxyl group has gained a proton
a positive charge on the carboxyl group
a net negative charge, because the amino group has lost its extra proton

questions.solution_md: In alkali the NH3+ group loses a proton, leaving COO−: net negative — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A protein is unusually rich in lysine and arginine. Near neutral pH it will tend to carry

options.text_md: a net negative charge, because they have extra carboxyl groups
no net charge, because all proteins are neutral
a charge decided only by its peptide bonds
a net positive charge, because these amino acids have extra basic groups

questions.solution_md: Lysine and arginine are basic amino acids — option (d).

questions.stem_md: People who live mainly on a cereal diet may lack lysine, which the human body cannot make. Lysine is therefore called
questions.solution_md: An amino acid that must be supplied by food is essential — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Aspartic acid and glutamic acid are called acidic amino acids because their R groups contain
questions.solution_md: An extra carboxyl group makes the amino acid acidic — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Glycine can be made by the human body.

**Reason (R):** Glycine has the simplest R group, a single hydrogen atom.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but being simple is not the reason it is non-essential: the body has the pathways to make it — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Glycine, cysteine and serine weigh 75, 121 and 105 daltons, and water 18. What is the mass of the tripeptide made of these three amino acids, each used once?
Four different amino acids are each used once to make a tetrapeptide. How many different tetrapeptides are possible?
questions.solution_md: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$ different orders.

questions.stem_md: Name the four groups attached to the central carbon atom of an amino acid, and say which of them differs from one amino acid to another.

answer.model_answer_md: The central (alpha) carbon carries an **amino group**, a **carboxyl group**, a **hydrogen atom** and an **R group**. Only the **R group** differs from one amino acid to another; for example it is H in glycine, CH₃ in alanine and CH₂OH in serine.

questions.solution_md: Four groups; R varies.

marking_scheme.step: R group varies, with an example

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between essential and non-essential amino acids, and give two examples of essential amino acids.

answer.model_answer_md: **Essential** amino acids **cannot be made by the body** and must be obtained from food; **non-essential** ones **can be made** by the body from other substances. Examples of essential amino acids are **lysine, methionine, valine, leucine, tryptophan** (any two).

questions.solution_md: Distinction; two examples.

marking_scheme.step: Two examples of essential amino acids

questions.stem_md: Classify amino acids on the basis of their R groups into four classes, with one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Neutral** amino acids have one amino and one carboxyl group, for example **glycine**. **Acidic** ones have an extra carboxyl group, for example **glutamic acid**. **Basic** ones have an extra basic group, for example **lysine**. **Sulphur-containing** ones carry sulphur in the R group, for example **cysteine**.

questions.solution_md: Four classes with examples.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw the structures of glycine, alanine and serine. [2]
(b) Explain why an amino acid exists as a zwitterion in water. [2]
(c) Name one essential and one non-essential amino acid. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** each has the central carbon bearing **H₂N–**, **–COOH**, **H** and an R group: **glycine** R = H, **alanine** R = CH₃, **serine** R = CH₂OH.

(b) In water the **carboxyl group** (acidic) **gives a proton** to the **amino group** (basic), so the molecule carries **NH₃⁺** and **COO⁻** at the same time: a **zwitterion** with **no net charge**; in acid it is positive and in alkali negative.

(c) **Essential**: lysine (or valine, methionine and others); **non-essential**: glycine, alanine or serine.

questions.solution_md: Three structures; zwitterion; examples.

questions.stem_md: The white of an egg turns solid and opaque when boiled. Which statement describes what has happened to its proteins?

options.text_md: Weak bonds were broken and the folded shape was lost, but the amino-acid sequence is unchanged.
The peptide bonds were broken and free amino acids formed.
The proteins were converted into carbohydrates.
The amino acids were rearranged into a new sequence.

questions.solution_md: Heat denatures a protein by disrupting its secondary and tertiary structure; the primary structure remains — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In sickle-cell haemoglobin, one glutamic acid of a chain is replaced by valine. Which level of protein structure is directly altered by this substitution?

options.text_md: None, because the number of chains is unchanged
The peptide bonds, which are all broken

questions.solution_md: A change of one amino acid changes the sequence, the primary structure — option (b).

options.text_md: peptide bonds between the amino acids
hydrogen bonds between groups of the backbone

questions.solution_md: D is a helix, the secondary structure, held by hydrogen bonds — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A denatured protein loses its biological activity.

**Reason (R):** Denaturation breaks the peptide bonds of the primary structure.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true, but the reason is false: denaturation breaks only the weak bonds that hold the folded shape, and the peptide bonds remain — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Replacing a single amino acid in a protein can change its function.

answer.model_answer_md: A different amino acid can alter the **folding** and so the **three-dimensional shape** of the protein, and function depends on shape.

questions.solution_md: Changes folding and shape.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy: Primary structure : sequence of amino acids :: Quaternary structure : ______

answer.model_answer_md: **Association of two or more folded polypeptide chains** (subunits).

questions.solution_md: Association of subunits.

questions.stem_md: A protein is made of three polypeptide chains containing 417 amino acids in all. How many peptide bonds does it have?
questions.solution_md: $417 - 3 = 414$ peptide bonds (one fewer than the number of amino acids in each chain).

questions.stem_md: Name the bond that stabilises the primary structure of a protein and the bond that stabilises its secondary structure.

answer.model_answer_md: The **primary structure** is held by **peptide bonds**, which are covalent bonds between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. The **secondary structure** (helix or sheet) is held by **hydrogen bonds** between groups of the backbone.

questions.solution_md: Peptide bonds; hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem_md: A student boils a solution of egg albumin and it turns cloudy. Explain what happens to the protein at the molecular level and say which level of structure is not changed.

answer.model_answer_md: Heat breaks the **weak hydrogen bonds, ionic and hydrophobic interactions** that hold the **secondary and tertiary structures**, so the protein **unfolds** and its **shape is lost** (it is **denatured**), which makes it clump and turn cloudy. The **primary structure** is not changed, because the **peptide bonds** are not broken.

questions.solution_md: Weak bonds broken; unfolded; primary unchanged.

questions.stem_md: Link each protein to its function: keratin, an antibody and myosin.

answer.model_answer_md: **Keratin** is a **structural protein** that gives strength to hair, nails and the outer skin. An **antibody** is a **defence protein** that binds a foreign substance and helps to remove it. **Myosin** is a **contractile protein** that, with actin, produces movement in muscle.

questions.solution_md: Three proteins and functions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the primary and the secondary structure of a protein, and name the bond that stabilises each. [2]
(b) Describe the tertiary and the quaternary structure, naming the bonds involved in the tertiary structure. [2]
(c) State one function each of keratin and haemoglobin. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Primary**: the **sequence of amino acids** in the chain, held by **peptide bonds**. **Secondary**: regular coiling into an **α-helix** or folding into a **β-pleated sheet**, held by **hydrogen bonds**.

(b) **Tertiary**: the **folding of the whole chain** into a three-dimensional shape, held by **hydrogen bonds, ionic and hydrophobic interactions and disulphide bridges** between cysteines. **Quaternary**: the **association of two or more folded chains** (subunits) in one protein, as in haemoglobin.

(c) **Keratin** gives **strength** to hair and skin; **haemoglobin** **carries oxygen** in the blood.

questions.solution_md: Four levels with bonds; functions.

questions.stem_md: Groundnut oil stays liquid on a cool morning, whereas butter is solid. The main reason is that groundnut oil has more

options.text_md: saturated fatty acids, whose straight chains pack closely
phosphate groups on its fatty acids
unsaturated fatty acids, whose double bonds bend the chains

questions.solution_md: Double bonds keep the chains of an unsaturated oil apart, so it stays liquid — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Fat gives about nine kilocalories per gram and carbohydrate about four. Which is the best reason why animals that must move about keep most of their reserve as fat?

options.text_md: Fat dissolves easily in water and can be carried by blood
A given mass of fat holds more than twice the energy, so the animal carries less weight
Fat contains nitrogen needed for muscles
Fat is hydrolysed faster than glycogen

questions.solution_md: 180 kcal from 20 g of fat against 80 kcal from 20 g of carbohydrate — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is not a lipid?
questions.solution_md: Inulin is a polysaccharide; the others are lipids — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy: Saturated fatty acid : no double bond :: Unsaturated fatty acid : ______

answer.model_answer_md: **One or more double bonds**.

questions.solution_md: One or more double bonds.

questions.stem_md: A fat has glycerol (92) joined to stearic acid (284), oleic acid (282) and palmitic acid (256). Using water = 18, find its molecular mass.
Distinguish between a fat and an oil, with reference to their state, fatty acids and usual source.

answer.model_answer_md: A **fat** is **solid** at room temperature, contains mostly **saturated** fatty acids with no double bonds, and is usually of **animal** origin. An **oil** is **liquid** at room temperature, contains many **unsaturated** fatty acids with double bonds, and is usually of **plant** origin.

questions.solution_md: State; fatty acids; source.

questions.stem_md: Classify lipids into three groups and give one example and one function for each group.

answer.model_answer_md: **Simple lipids**, such as **fats and oils**, are esters of fatty acids and glycerol and **store energy**. **Compound lipids**, such as **phospholipids**, contain a phosphate group and **form the bilayer of cell membranes**. **Derived lipids**, such as **cholesterol and other steroids**, are made from simple or compound lipids and act in membranes or as **hormones**.

questions.solution_md: Three groups with examples and functions.

questions.stem_md: State three functions of lipids in the body of an animal, naming the kind of lipid concerned in each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Fats** store energy, giving more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, and form an **insulating layer** under the skin that reduces heat loss and cushions organs. **Phospholipids and cholesterol** are the main components of **cell membranes**, which are built on a bilayer. **Steroids**, such as the sex hormones, act as **chemical messengers** that regulate growth and reproduction.

questions.solution_md: Three functions.

marking_scheme.step: Energy store or insulation by fats

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw the structure of a triglyceride, showing glycerol, the ester bonds and fatty acids. [2]
(b) How do saturated and unsaturated fatty acids differ in structure, and what effect does this have on the state of the fat? [2]
(c) Name one lipid that forms membranes. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a **glycerol** molecule with three carbons, each joined through an **ester bond** (–O–CO–) to one of **three fatty acid chains**; three water molecules are lost.

(b) A **saturated** fatty acid has **no double bonds**, so its chain is **straight** and the molecules pack closely, giving a **solid fat**. An **unsaturated** fatty acid has **one or more double bonds** that **bend** the chain, so the molecules pack loosely, giving a **liquid oil**.

(c) A **phospholipid** (or cholesterol).

questions.solution_md: Triglyceride; saturated and unsaturated; membrane lipid.

questions.stem_md: Lactate dehydrogenase removes two hydrogen atoms from lactate to form pyruvate. To which class does this enzyme belong?
questions.solution_md: Removing hydrogen is an oxidation, catalysed by an oxidoreductase — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A person who lacks niacin cannot make enough NAD, and many dehydrogenase enzymes fail. In these enzymes NAD acts as a
questions.solution_md: NAD is a loosely bound organic cofactor made from a vitamin, a coenzyme — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Relative activities at 5, 15 and 25 °C were measured for two enzymes: enzyme X 37, 100, 0; enzyme Y 8, 30, 70. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text_md: Enzyme X is probably from a mammal, because it is active at low temperature.
Enzyme X is probably from a polar fish: its optimum is near 15 °C and it is inactive at 25 °C.
Enzyme Y has its optimum below 15 °C.
Both enzymes have the same optimum temperature.

questions.solution_md: X peaks at 15 °C and is lost at 25 °C, as expected of a cold-adapted enzyme, while Y is still rising at 25 °C — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A mixture contains pepsin, whose optimum is near pH 2, and trypsin, whose optimum is near pH 8. At pH 3 the relative activities are 37 for one and 0 for the other. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Pepsin is the active enzyme, because pH 3 is close to its optimum.
Trypsin is the active enzyme, because it prefers weak acid.
Neither can work at any pH below 7.

questions.solution_md: Pepsin keeps 37 percent of its maximum at pH 3 and trypsin 0 — option (a).

options.text_md: remain far below the original maximum
almost reach the same maximum as without the inhibitor

questions.solution_md: The substrate outcompetes the inhibitor: at a concentration of 1000 the rate is 79.2 without and 78.4 with it — option (c).

questions.solution_md: F lies below E at every substrate concentration but approaches the same maximum — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A competitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction.

**Reason (R):** A competitive inhibitor binds permanently to the enzyme.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: the maximum rate is unchanged, and the binding is reversible so more substrate displaces the inhibitor — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The activity of most enzymes falls sharply above about 50 °C.

answer.model_answer_md: The enzyme protein is **denatured**: heat breaks the weak bonds that hold its shape, so the **active site is lost**.

questions.solution_md: Denaturation.

questions.stem_md: An enzyme has a maximum rate of 80 units and a Michaelis constant of 10 units of substrate. Using $v = \dfrac{V_{\max} S}{K_m + S}$, find the rate at a substrate concentration of 30 units.
questions.solution_md: $v = \dfrac{80 \times 30}{10 + 30} = 60$ units.

questions.stem_md: With a competitive inhibitor the same enzyme behaves as if its Michaelis constant were 20, with the maximum unchanged at 80. Find the rate at a substrate concentration of 50 units, to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: $v = \dfrac{80 \times 50}{20 + 50} = 57.1$ units, against 66.7 without the inhibitor.

questions.stem_md: Methanol is converted by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase into a toxic product. Patients with methanol poisoning are given ethanol. Explain, using competitive inhibition, why this helps.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ethanol** is a **better-fitting substrate** of alcohol dehydrogenase and **competes** with methanol for the **active site**. The enzyme is mostly occupied by ethanol, so **less methanol is converted** into the toxic product and it can be excreted.

questions.solution_md: Competition for the active site.

marking_scheme.step: Ethanol competes for the active site

questions.stem_md: State four properties of enzymes.

answer.model_answer_md: Enzymes are **biological catalysts** that **lower the activation energy**; they are **specific** for a substrate through the **active site**; they are **not used up** in the reaction; and they are **sensitive to temperature and pH**, being **denatured** by extremes. They are mostly **proteins**.

questions.solution_md: Four properties.

questions.stem_md: Name the six classes of enzymes and state the type of reaction catalysed by any three of them.

answer.model_answer_md: The six classes are **oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases**. **Oxidoreductases**, such as lactate dehydrogenase, catalyse **oxidation and reduction**; **transferases**, such as hexokinase, **transfer a group** such as phosphate from one molecule to another; **hydrolases**, such as lipase, **split bonds by adding water**.

questions.solution_md: Six classes; three reactions.

questions.stem_md: An enzyme extract loses all its activity after dialysis, but activity returns when the small molecules that passed out are added back. Name the type of component that was lost and distinguish it from a prosthetic group.

answer.model_answer_md: The lost component is a **coenzyme**, a small **organic cofactor** that is **loosely bound** and can pass through the dialysis membrane. A **prosthetic group** is also an organic cofactor, but it is **tightly bound** to the enzyme and would **not be removed** by dialysis. The protein alone is the apoenzyme and with its cofactor the holoenzyme.

questions.solution_md: Coenzyme; loosely against tightly bound.

questions.stem_md: Explain the shape of a graph of enzyme activity against temperature, from low temperature through the optimum to high temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: At **low temperature** molecules have little energy, so the rate is **low** (the enzyme is not destroyed). As the temperature rises, **collisions between enzyme and substrate** become more frequent and the rate **rises** to the **optimum**. Beyond the optimum the enzyme is **denatured**, its shape is lost and the rate **falls sharply**.

questions.solution_md: Rise, optimum, fall.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is competitive inhibition? Explain it with the example of malonate and succinic dehydrogenase. [3]
(b) Draw a graph of rate against substrate concentration, with and without a competitive inhibitor. [1]
(c) How can the effect of the inhibitor be reduced? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In **competitive inhibition** a molecule that **resembles the substrate** occupies the **active site** of the enzyme and **blocks it**. **Malonate** looks like **succinate**, the substrate of **succinic dehydrogenase**, so it binds to the active site and **reduces the conversion of succinate to fumarate**. The binding is **reversible**.

(b) **Graph:** two rising curves that level off; the curve **with the inhibitor lies below** the other at low and moderate substrate concentration, but both approach the **same maximum**.

(c) By **raising the substrate concentration**, which **outcompetes** the inhibitor for the active site.

questions.solution_md: A glycosidic bond forms with the loss of one water: 2 × 180 − 18 = 342 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of amino acids contains sulphur?
questions.solution_md: Cysteine and methionine are the sulphur-containing amino acids — option (c).

options.text_md: One molecule of water is released as the peptide bond forms.
Two molecules of water are released.
One molecule of water is taken up.
No water is released or taken up.

questions.solution_md: The mass is 75 + 89 − 18 = 146 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A kinase works only when magnesium ions are present. When they are removed with a chelating agent the enzyme stops, and it recovers when they are added back. Magnesium acts as

options.text_md: a metal-ion cofactor that activates the enzyme
a coenzyme made from a vitamin

questions.solution_md: Metal ions such as magnesium and zinc are cofactors — option (c).

questions.stem_md: An enzyme converts glucose 6-phosphate into fructose 6-phosphate, which has the same formula. To which class does it belong?
questions.solution_md: Rearrangement into an isomer is catalysed by an isomerase — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The latex of the opium poppy contains morphine, which the plant does not need for its growth or respiration. Morphine is
questions.solution_md: Morphine is a nitrogen-containing alkaloid and a secondary metabolite — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The red colour of beetroot and the purple of red cabbage come from anthocyanins. In plant chemistry, anthocyanins are

options.text_md: secondary metabolites of the pigment group

questions.solution_md: Pigments such as anthocyanins are secondary metabolites — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Many plants make alkaloids although the alkaloids are not needed for their basic metabolism.

answer.model_answer_md: Alkaloids help the plant in other ways, for example by **deterring herbivores** or by **protecting against microbes**.

questions.solution_md: Defence.

questions.stem_md: What are secondary metabolites? Give two examples from different groups.

answer.model_answer_md: **Secondary metabolites** are compounds that are **not directly needed for the growth, development or reproduction** of an organism, but are useful to it in other ways, for example for defence or attraction. Examples are the **alkaloid morphine** and the **pigment anthocyanin** (or **gum arabic**).

questions.solution_md: Definition; two examples.

questions.stem_md: Give one example each of an alkaloid, a pigment and a gum, and state a use or role of each.

answer.model_answer_md: An **alkaloid** such as **quinine** is used as a medicine against malaria and defends the plant. A **pigment** such as **carotenoid or anthocyanin** gives colour to petals and fruits and **attracts pollinators or animals that spread seeds**. **Gum arabic** from Acacia **seals wounds** in the plant and is used in food and industry.

questions.solution_md: Three examples with uses.

questions.passage_md:
The initial rate of an enzyme reaction was measured at six substrate concentrations, with and without a competitive inhibitor (units are arbitrary).

| Substrate | Rate without inhibitor | Rate with inhibitor |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 26.7 | 16 |
| 10 | 40 | 26.7 |
| 20 | 53.3 | 40 |
| 50 | 66.7 | 57.1 |
| 100 | 72.7 | 66.7 |
| 200 | 76.2 | 72.7 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 33.3 %

**(b)** (a) The inhibitor is competitive: its effect becomes small at a high substrate concentration.

**(c)** (i) The uninhibited rate is half of its maximum (40) at a concentration of **10**, the Michaelis constant. With the competitive inhibitor the same rate (40) needs a concentration of **20**, so the concentration **increases** while the maximum rate is unchanged.

**OR** (ii) The maximum rate would **roughly double**, because there are **twice as many active sites** available to work on the substrate at the same time.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{40 - 26.7}{40} \times 100 = 33.3$ percent.

**(b)** The rates differ by 10.7 at 5 but only by 3.5 at 200, so substrate overcomes the inhibitor — option (a).

**(c)** (i) 10; rises to 20.

(ii) Doubles; more active sites.

questions.passage_md: A student makes a pentapeptide by joining the amino acids serine, glycine, cysteine, alanine and cysteine in this order, using the masses serine 105, glycine 75, cysteine 121, alanine 89 daltons (cysteine is used twice) and water 18.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 439 daltons

**(b)** (b) The two cysteine residues, by a disulphide bridge

**(c)** (i) It contains **4 peptide bonds** (one fewer than the number of amino acids). **Serine** has a hydroxyl group in its R group (CH₂OH).

**OR** (ii) **Cysteine** is a **sulphur-containing** amino acid and **glycine** a **neutral** one. The R group of cysteine is **CH₂SH** and contains sulphur, whereas that of glycine is **only a hydrogen atom**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Sum of residues $= 511$; four waters are lost: $511 - 4 \times 18 = 439$.

**(b)** Two cysteines can be joined by an S–S bridge — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Four; serine.

(ii) Sulphur-containing; neutral; R groups.
